270	### Learning 293: YAML Frontmatter Markdown > JSON for Cross-Platform Config
271	Initial implementation used JSON for `learned-budgets.json`. Switched to YAML frontmatter markdown (`.md`) because: (1) consistent with vault cerebellum/, skills/*.md, .context/skills/ patterns; (2) vault-keeper and Obsidian can index YAML frontmatter; (3) markdown body carries narrative context (why budgets were learned, which sessions contributed); (4) any tool (Zed, Pi, humans) can read markdown naturally. JSON reserved for wire formats (MCP responses, API payloads) and high-frequency machine-to-machine data. Codified as coding standard in `.claude/rules/common-coding-style.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.
272	
273	### Learning 294: Instance-Level Dicts Prevent Module-Level Singleton Pollution
274	`ContextPolicy._load_learned_budgets()` initially mutated the module-level `_PROFILE_BUDGETS` dict. This caused test pollution: one test loading custom budgets permanently changed defaults for all subsequent tests in the same process (exact pattern from L290/Session 56). Fix: `self._budgets = dict(_PROFILE_BUDGETS)` creates an instance-level copy at init time. `get_budget()` and `save_learned_budgets()` read/write `self._budgets`. General rule: any module-level mutable state that gets modified at runtime must be copied to instance scope. The module-level dict becomes an immutable template.
275	
276	### Learning 295: SurrealDB 3.0 SELECT VALUE for Scalar Subqueries
277	`WHERE field IN (SELECT col FROM table)` returns 0 matches in SurrealDB 3.0 because `SELECT col` returns records `[{col: "val"}]`, not scalars `["val"]`. Must use `SELECT VALUE col` to get a flat array. This caused Graph HIHO's orphan ratio to falsely read 1.000 (every neuron appeared orphaned despite 5,119 synapses existing). Pattern: always use `SELECT VALUE` in `IN` subqueries. Applies to all SurrealDB 3.0+ code.
278	
279	### Learning 296: Aspirational Test Specs Must Target Existing APIs
280	`TestExecuteGraphWiring` tested `ExecutionOrchestrator.execute_graph()` which was never implemented. Tests failed with `AttributeError` for months as a pre-existing failure. Fix: rewrite to use `GraphEngine.execute()` which actually exists and provides the same FLUX integration. Pattern: forward-looking test specs are fine, but they must be marked `@pytest.mark.skip(reason="API not yet implemented")` or target the existing API that provides equivalent functionality.

### Learning 293: YAML Frontmatter Markdown > JSON for Cross-Platform Config
Initial implementation used JSON for `learned-budgets.json`. Switched to YAML frontmatter markdown (`.md`) because: (1) consistent with vault cerebellum/, skills/*.md, .context/skills/ patterns; (2) vault-keeper and Obsidian can index YAML frontmatter; (3) markdown body carries narrative context (why budgets were learned, which sessions contributed); (4) any tool (Zed, Pi, humans) can read markdown naturally. JSON reserved for wire formats (MCP responses, API payloads) and high-frequency machine-to-machine data. Codified as coding standard in `.claude/rules/common-coding-style.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.

### Learning 294: Instance-Level Dicts Prevent Module-Level Singleton Pollution
`ContextPolicy._load_learned_budgets()` initially mutated the module-level `_PROFILE_BUDGETS` dict. This caused test pollution: one test loading custom budgets permanently changed defaults for all subsequent tests in the same process (exact pattern from L290/Session 56). Fix: `self._budgets = dict(_PROFILE_BUDGETS)` creates an instance-level copy at init time. `get_budget()` and `save_learned_budgets()` read/write `self._budgets`. General rule: any module-level mutable state that gets modified at runtime must be copied to instance scope. The module-level dict becomes an immutable template.

### Learning 295: SurrealDB 3.0 SELECT VALUE for Scalar Subqueries
`WHERE field IN (SELECT col FROM table)` returns 0 matches in SurrealDB 3.0 because `SELECT col` returns records `[{col: "val"}]`, not scalars `["val"]`. Must use `SELECT VALUE col` to get a flat array. This caused Graph HIHO's orphan ratio to falsely read 1.000 (every neuron appeared orphaned despite 5,119 synapses existing). Pattern: always use `SELECT VALUE` in `IN` subqueries. Applies to all SurrealDB 3.0+ code.

### Learning 296: Aspirational Test Specs Must Target Existing APIs
`TestExecuteGraphWiring` tested `ExecutionOrchestrator.execute_graph()` which was never implemented. Tests failed with `AttributeError` for months as a pre-existing failure. ### Learning 296: Aspirational Test Specs Must Target Existing APIs

Pattern: forward-looking test specs are fine, but they must be marked `@pytest.mark.skip(reason="API not yet implemented")` or target the existing API that provides equivalent functionality.

### Learning 297: Tiered Proactivity for Autonomous Monitoring (Session 96b)
Built Anthropic Intelligence Feed: 11-source registry, version-watch SessionStart hook, `/anthropic-scan` command, risk-tiered auto-integration. Key architecture insight: **three feedback loops** — Push (version-watch hook, instant local check every session), Pull (`/anthropic-scan` on-demand deep scan), Persist (vault routing for research/decisions). Staleness check (>24h) triggers background agent scan automatically. Different sources need different action types: CLI changelog → config edits, API deprecations → code changes, research papers → vault knowledge. Risk tiers: low (auto-apply with batch confirm), medium (per-item confirm), high (report only).

### Learning 298: Deprecated Model IDs Are Silent Failures
`api_llm_executor.py` had `claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022` and `claude-3-opus-20240229` — both retired months ago. Tests passed because they don't make live API calls, but any production use would return HTTP errors. The `/anthropic-scan` system now includes model deprecation checking against `api-manifest.json` to catch these proactively. Pattern: model IDs in cost tables and defaults must be treated as **versioned dependencies** — they expire and need periodic refresh, just like package versions.

### Learning 299: Auto-Integration Needs Risk Classification
Not all new features should be auto-applied. Env vars and Bash permissions are safe (low risk), but hook types and API behavior changes can break workflows (medium/high risk). The auto-integration engine classifies by risk tier and adjusts confirmation behavior accordingly. This prevents both "never updated" drift and "broke everything" over-eagerness. All changes logged to `change-log.md` for audit trail.

A central registry of the swarm's **6-Dimensional Service Architecture**. Only "Prime" skills are listed here.

## 4. PHYSICS (Genesis Engine — Grounded Simulation)
*The Body: 12D Riemannian Manifold with Real Mathematics.*
- **Spinor**: SU(2) algebra, Bloch sphere, HIHO = equatorial state (`physics/spinor.py`).
- **Geometry**: Riemannian metric, Christoffel symbols, geodesics (`physics/riemannian_metric.py`).
- **Dynamics**: Euler-Lagrange, symplectic Verlet integrator (`physics/lagrangian.py`).
- **Bundle**: Fiber bundle P(B⁴,SO(3)⁴), parallel transport (`physics/fiber_bundle.py`).
- **Gauge**: Yang-Mills SO(3), covariant Tempic field (`physics/gauge_theory.py`).
- **Fisher**: Information geometry, Rosetta Stone metric (`physics/information_geometry.py`).
- **Cosmogony**: Landau phase transitions ∅→HIHO, Brahmagupta's zero (`physics/cosmogony.py`).
- **MHD/HIHO**: HIHOUnifiedEngine with 11 sub-engines (`universe/hiho_unified_engine.py`).

- **World Model**: JEPA 86K-param predictor + surprise explorer (`world_model/`).

- **Research**: [Paper draft](docs/papers/genesis-engine-paper.md) | [Research doc](docs/genesis-engine-research.md) | [Tutorials](docs/tutorials/).

*The Brain: Model Routing & Learning.*
- **Routing**: [MODEL_ROUTING_PRIME](file:///home/mike-anderson/dev/cohezion/src/cohezion/skills/MODEL_ROUTING_PRIME.md).
- **TDA Routing**: TopologicalRouter — H₀/H₁ → exploit/explore/pivot (`swarm/topological_router.py`).
- **Data**: [TRAINING_DATA_CAPTURE_PRIME](file:///home/mike-anderson/dev/cohezion/src/cohezion/skills/TRAINING_DATA_CAPTURE_PRIME.md).

- **Autoresearch**: `AutoresearchDriver` (K-Search UCB1, subprocess eval, SurrealDB persist) at `research/autoresearch_driver.py`. Dispatched via Step 5.91 in `CompoundExecutor.execute_task()` on keywords: train/optimize/research/experiment/tune/improve loss. K-Search trees at `~/.cohezion-research/ksearch/{target}.json`. Targets: jepa/flume_vae/rl_ppo.
- **A2A Discovery**: `GET /agents` returns all registered specialist agents via `CapabilityRegistry._scan_claude_agents()` (scans `.claude/agents/*.md` YAML frontmatter).

## 6. INFRASTRUCTURE (VLIW Service)
*The Substrate: Hardware & Data.*
- **Database**: [DATABASE_PRIME](file:///home/mike-anderson/dev/cohezion/src/cohezion/skills/DATABASE_PRIME.md) (SurrealDB).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Retrospective summary — what the compound loop learned this session:**

1. **Autonomous monitoring is a reusable architecture pattern.** The 11-source registry + risk-tiered auto-integration + tiered proactivity (push/pull/persist) model applies beyond Anthropic. The same pattern could monitor Python ecosystem releases, SurrealDB updates, or Ollama model availability.

2. **Model IDs are versioned dependencies.** `api_llm_executor.py` had silently retired model IDs that would have failed in production. This is the same class of problem as pinning to a deleted npm package — it needs automated detection, not manual remembering.

3. **Documentation drifts fastest at the meta level.** The code (6,184 tests pass) was current, but CLAUDE.md had no mention of the session's biggest deliverable. The retrospective caught this before it compounded.

def compute_coherence(self) -> HolographicCoherenceReport:

    boundary_coherence = []
    for i in range(len(self._shards) - 1):
        shard_a = self._shards[i]
        shard_b = self._shards[i + 1]
        if shard_a.data and shard_b.data:
            # Boundary coherence: last dim of A ~ first dim of B
            diff = abs(shard_a.data[-1] - shard_b.data[0])
            # HIHO sigmoid formula (lines 141):

        total_dims=sum(s.size for s in self._shards),
        coherence_score=round(score, 4),
        pointer_flips=self._pointer_flips,
    )

# The Cohezion Charter

This document defines the specialized behavioral, simulation, and orchestration frameworks unique to the **Cohezion** platform. It serves as an expansion of the core [CONSTITUTION.md](file:///home/mike-anderson/dev/cohezion/.agent/CONSTITUTION.md), enabling expert universe simulation and multi-domain problem solving.

## 1. The 0.5 Coherence Rule (HIHO Stability)
This is the foundational principle of reality precipitation within the Cohezion universe.
- **Concept**: Maximum stability in the manifesting of reality (precipitation) occurs at exactly the **50% (0.5) coherence overlap**.
- **Mechanics**: Stability is achieved when "Internal Intent" and "External Environment" reach a state of Half-In-Half-Out (HIHO) balance.
- **Mathematical Grounding** (Session 74): HIHO = Brahmagupta's zero (δ = coherence - 0.5 = 0), Friston's free energy minimum (F = E - TS), flat gauge connection (F = 0), Fisher metric minimum, and Bloch sphere equator (⟨σ_z⟩ = 0). Six perspectives on the same mathematical object. See `docs/genesis-engine-research.md` and `physics/cosmogony.py`.

## 2. The Fundamental Unit of SPIN
Reality is structured through toroidal momentum.
- **SPIN**: The fundamental unit of information and particle formation, consisting of both **Rotation** and **Precession**.
- **Coherence**: When rotation and precession are aligned, stability increases. Charge polarity is a resultant of these coherent fields.
- **Mathematical Grounding** (Session 74): SPIN is now implemented as proper SU(2) spinor algebra on the Bloch sphere. Rotation = ⟨σ_x⟩, Precession = ⟨σ_y⟩, Charge = ⟨σ_z⟩ (Pauli expectation values). HIHO state = (|↑⟩+|↓⟩)/√2 (equatorial). See `physics/spinor.py`.

## 3. FLUME Evolution (Latent Trajectories)
The **FLUME** (Fluid Latent Understanding through Manifold Encoding) methodology enables revolutionary thought navigation.
- **Latent Trajectories**: Mapping semantic momentum in 256D latent spaces to predict and guide conceptual evolution.
- **Manifold Reasoning**: Moving beyond linear token prediction to 12D state vectors and manifold-based understanding.
- **Mathematical Grounding** (Session 74): The Fisher information metric on FLUME's latent space is the Rosetta Stone — it simultaneously defines the Riemannian metric for dynamics, the thermodynamic metric, and the optimal 256D→12D projection. Agent trajectories follow Euler-Lagrange geodesics on a fabric-block metric with Yang-Mills gauge fields. See `physics/information_geometry.py`, `physics/lagrangian.py`, `physics/gauge_theory.py`.

## 4. Abstraction as Primary (Paradox of Minutiae)
Avoid the "Paradox of Minutiae" by prioritizing high-level conceptual maps.
- **Strategy**: Leverage "Golden Mean" attractors and foundational patterns over mechanistic details.
- **Growth Loop**: Use these abstractions to synthesize new knowledge into the 12D manifold, ensuring that every learning improves the system's global capability.
- **Grounding**: All simulations must be grounded in the Charter pillars before detail is precipitated.

## 5. Sovereignty & Transparency (Observable AI)
Maintain absolute transparency in swarm operations.
- **Transparency**: Expose internal states, FLUME trajectories, and confidence levels *before* action.
- **Human-in-the-Loop**: Position agents as high-fidelity universe simulators, with humans as the ultimate orchestrators and reality anchors.

## 6. Deterministic Responsibility (Idempotency)
Ensure predictability in a complex agents-of-agents ecosystem.
- **Idempotency**: All significant agentic actions must use idempotency keys to ensure stable, reproducible, and verifiable outcomes.

## 7. Recursive Capability Evolution
Enable a continuous growth loop for the swarm.
- **Knowledge Assimilation**: Proactively apply abstractions to incorporate multi-domain discoveries into the knowledge graph.
- **Skill Refinement**: Periodically review and refactor skills based on retrospective analysis, ensuring the swarm's capabilities evolve as the mission complexity increases.

## 8. Expert Domain Lattice (EDL)
The primary reasoning engine for COHEZION is the **Expert Domain Lattice**, coordinated by the **Quadrature Nexus Orchestration**.
- **The Expert Streams**: All complex problems must be routed through five specialized streams: Architect (Design), Engineer (Physics), Biologist (Life), Quantum Hardware (Hardware), and Quantum Algo (Compute). Each stream evaluates proposals independently, producing a `StreamRecommendation` with confidence and coherence scores.
- **Consensus Stabilization**: Trajectories are considered stable only when consensus is reached across the EDL, adhering to the 0.5 Coherence Rule. The `EDLConsensus` model reports `hiho_stable: bool` (coherence within 0.4-0.6) and `consensus_strength` (1.0 = perfect HIHO alignment).
- **Quadrature Nexus**: The 4-voice consensus mechanism (Architect, Engineer, Ethicist, Resource) gates all major swarm actions. Action is taken only when alignment exceeds 0.85. Grounded in Percival's Triune Self and Noether's theorem (consensus symmetry → action conservation).
- **Triune Consensus**: The geometric equilibrium of Architect, Engineer, and Biologist proposals in 12D state space. KL Divergence validates the 512D→12D projection fidelity.
- **Implementation**: `platform/edl_router.py` (5-stream routing), `swarm/quadrature_nexus.py` (4-voice governance), `swarm/triune_consensus.py` (geometric equilibrium).

"""Graph health computation logic tied to HIHO equilibrium."""


def compute_graph_hiho(metrics: dict) -> float:
    """Weighted average graph health score.

    Weights: connectivity 0.3, reciprocity 0.2, freshness 0.2, (1 - orphan_ratio) 0.3.
    Target: 0.5 +/- 0.15 (HIHO equilibrium).
    """
    connectivity = metrics.get("connectivity", 0.0)
    reciprocity = metrics.get("reciprocity", 0.0)
    freshness = metrics.get("freshness", 0.0)
    orphan_ratio = metrics.get("orphan_ratio", 1.0)

    return 0.3 * connectivity + 0.2 * reciprocity + 0.2 * freshness + 0.3 * (1.0 - orphan_ratio)


def classify_health(score: float) -> str:
    """Classify graph health based on HIHO equilibrium distance.

    - healthy:  0.35 <= score <= 0.65
    - degraded: 0.2 <= score < 0.35 or 0.65 < score <= 0.8
    - critical: score < 0.2 or score > 0.8
    """
    if score < 0.2 or score > 0.8:
        return "critical"
    if score < 0.35 or score > 0.65:
        return "degraded"
    return "healthy"

"""Pre-configured compound client factory.

Creates a fully-wired :class:`TokenEfficientClient` with:
- :class:`SmartRouterAdapter` for intelligent model selection
- :class:`ContextHarness` for prompt pruning (target: phi3:mini)
- :class:`ResilientOllamaClient` for circuit-breaker-protected Ollama calls

Usage::

    client = get_compound_client()
    response = await client.generate("Analyze this code", task_type="coding")
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import Any

from cohezion.concurrency.safe_singleton import safe_singleton


logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def create_compound_client(
    strategy: str = "efficiency",
    ollama_host: str = "http://localhost:11434",
    cache_max_size: int = 512,
) -> Any:
    """Create a new :class:`TokenEfficientClient` wired with SmartRouter.

    Parameters
    ----------
    strategy : str
        SmartRouter strategy: ``"efficiency"``, ``"quality"``, or ``"speed"``.
    ollama_host : str
        Ollama API base URL.
    cache_max_size : int
        Maximum prompt-response cache entries.

    Returns
    -------
    TokenEfficientClient
        Fully wired client ready for live Ollama calls.
    """
    from cohezion.reliability.context_harness import ContextHarness
    from cohezion.swarm.model_adapter import SmartRouterAdapter
    from cohezion.swarm.smart_router import SmartRouter
    from cohezion.swarm.token_client import TokenEfficientClient

    # 1. SmartRouter with full LOCAL_MODELS registry
    smart_router = SmartRouter(
        ollama_host=ollama_host,
        strategy=strategy,
        log_actions=True,
    )

    # 2. Adapter for TokenEfficientClient's _router interface
    adapter = SmartRouterAdapter(smart_router)

## Phase 4: Graph HIHO Recalculation

### Task 4.1: Trigger graph_health via maintenance MCP

The `graph_health` MCP tool (`cohezion-maintenance-mcp/server.py:74`) queries SurrealDB for:
- Total neurons (from `neurons` table)
- Total synapses (from `synapses` table)
- Orphan ratio (neurons with no synapses)
- Connectivity (avg synapses per neuron)
- Reciprocity (bidirectional link ratio)
- Freshness (neurons updated within 7 days / total)

Then computes: `HIHO = 0.3 * connectivity + 0.2 * reciprocity + 0.2 * freshness + 0.3 * (1 - orphan_ratio)`

**Action:** Call the MCP tool directly, or run the equivalent SurrealDB queries manually:

SELECT count() AS c FROM synapses GROUP ALL;

# Plan: Complete Backlog Items from Retrospective

## Context

**Problem:** The Session 96b retrospective identified 4 remaining items that need attention. After deep investigation, one item (CONSTITUTION.md Section 8) was confirmed complete — reducing the backlog to 3 real items plus a recalculation.

**Corrected scope after investigation:**
- CONSTITUTION.md Section 8 is **NOT truncated** — confirmed complete at 75 lines with 10 compound engineering principles. Removed from backlog.
- COHEZION_CHARTER.md Section 8 (EDL) is genuinely incomplete — 7 lines covering 4 concepts but missing failure modes, consensus mechanics, and recovery patterns.
- `cost_aware_router.py` hardcoded dicts are **Ollama + Gemini only** (no Anthropic models). Dynamic model discovery needs the Ollama API and Gemini API, not the Anthropic Models API.
- Prompt caching applies only to `api_llm_executor.py` (the Anthropic fallback path), not the main compound loop (which goes through Ollama).
- Graph HIHO is calculated via `cohezion-maintenance-mcp/graph_health.py:compute_graph_hiho()` — can be triggered via the MCP `graph_health` tool.

---

## Phase 1: Complete COHEZION_CHARTER.md Section 8 (EDL)

### Task 1.1: Expand EDL failure modes and consensus mechanics

**File:** `.agent/COHEZION_CHARTER.md` (currently 49 lines)

The current Section 8 defines 4 concepts (Expert Streams, Consensus Stabilization, Quadrature Nexus, Triune Consensus) in 7 lines but lacks operational specifics. Add:

**Failure Modes** (new subsection after Implementation line):
- **Stream Disagreement**: When 2+ streams produce conflicting recommendations (confidence divergence >0.3), escalate to Quadrature Nexus for arbitration
- **Consensus Timeout**: If alignment score doesn't reach 0.85 within budget, fall back to highest-confidence single stream with a logged degradation event
- **Coherence Collapse**: If `hiho_stable` drops to false (coherence outside 0.4-0.6 band), freeze action, trigger Ouroboros self-healing, and re-query after stabilization
- **Single-stream Domination**: If one stream consistently overrides others (>80% of decisions), flag as lattice imbalance and force rotation

**Consensus Mechanics** (expand Quadrature Nexus bullet):
- Voting: Weighted by domain relevance (Architect weighs more on design decisions, Engineer on physics)
- Tiebreaker: Default to Engineer stream (physics grounding), unless Ethicist vetoes (hard constraint)
- Resource stream: Evaluates compute budget, token cost, and latency SLA — can veto expensive proposals

**12D Projection** (expand Triune Consensus bullet):
- Each stream's 512D recommendation is projected to 12D state space via the Fisher information metric
- Equilibrium: Proposals are "in consensus" when pairwise KL divergence < 0.1 nats in the 12D projection
- The 12D representation aligns with the FLUME manifold dimensions (Section 3)

**Recovery Patterns** (new subsection):
- Re-query: Retry with additional context injected from the disagreeing stream's reasoning
- Fallback: Degrade to single-stream routing (highest confidence) with logging
- Escalate: Surface to human when consensus fails 3 consecutive times on the same decision class

**Reuse:** Reference existing implementations at `platform/edl_router.py`, `swarm/quadrature_nexus.py`, `swarm/triune_consensus.py`.

---

## Phase 2: Dynamic Model Discovery in CostAwareRouter

### Task 2.1: Replace hardcoded Ollama model dicts with dynamic discovery

**File:** `src/cohezion/swarm/cost_aware_router.py`

The 5 hardcoded class-level dicts (`MODEL_COSTS`, `MODEL_QUALITY`, `MODEL_TPS`, `MODEL_LATENCY`, `MODEL_CONTEXT_LIMITS`) at lines 284-344, 551-562 contain 7 Ollama + 3 Gemini models. Replace with dynamic discovery:

**Ollama models:** Query `http://localhost:11434/api/tags` (Ollama REST API) at router initialization to get the list of locally available models. For each model, populate:
- `cost`: Always 0.0 (local)
- `context_limit`: From model metadata (`/api/show` endpoint returns `num_ctx`)
- `quality` and `tps`: Keep as a static lookup table — these are empirically measured, not API-discoverable

**Gemini models:** Keep as a static config dict (Gemini has no public model-listing API equivalent). The Gemini model list changes rarely (quarterly).

**Architecture:**
1. Move static quality/tps/latency scores to a YAML config file: `config/model_profiles.yaml`
2. At `__init__`, merge static profiles with dynamic Ollama discovery
3. Cache the merged result with a TTL (e.g., 5 minutes) — don't query Ollama on every routing decision
4. Fall back to hardcoded defaults if Ollama API is unreachable (resilience)

**Impact:** When a new Ollama model is pulled (`ollama pull`), it automatically appears in the router on next TTL expiry. No code change needed.

**Risk:** Medium. Router initialization adds an HTTP call. Mitigated by cache + fallback.

### Task 2.2: Add model profiles config file

**New file:** `config/model_profiles.yaml`

YAML frontmatter markdown with:
```yaml
---
version: "1.0.0"
last_updated: "2026-04-10"
---

# Model Profiles — empirically measured quality/speed/latency

ollama:
  phi3:mini:
    quality: 0.6
    tps: 15.0
    latency_ms: 50
  qwen3-coder:32b:
    quality: 0.85
    tps: 8.0
    latency_ms: 100
  # ... etc

gemini:
  gemini-2.0-flash-lite:
    quality: 0.70
    cost_per_1k: 0.000075
    tps: 50.0
    context_limit: 1000000
  # ... etc
```

---

## Phase 3: Anthropic Prompt Caching in API Executor

### Task 3.1: Add cache_control to api_llm_executor.py

**File:** `src/cohezion/integrations/agentverse/api_llm_executor.py`

The `_execute_anthropic()` method (lines 198-250) makes direct `httpx` calls to `api.anthropic.com/v1/messages`. Add `cache_control` to the system prompt when one is provided:

```python
# Current (line 216-224):
payload = {
    "model": self.model,
    "max_tokens": max_tokens,
    "temperature": temperature,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
}
if system:
    payload["system"] = system

# Updated:
if system:
    payload["system"] = [
        {"type": "text", "text": system, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}
    ]
```

This enables Anthropic's automatic caching — repeated calls with the same system prompt reuse cached tokens (up to 90% savings on input tokens). The `ephemeral` type means cache lives for the session duration.

**Also update:** `anthropic-version` header from `"2023-06-01"` to `"2024-01-01"` or later to ensure cache_control support.

**Risk:** Low. Additive change. Falls back to no-cache if header version is too old.

### Task 3.2: Evaluate advisor tool for compound loop

**No code changes.** Create an evaluation document at `docs/evaluations/advisor-tool-evaluation.md` that:
- Describes the advisor tool beta (`advisor-tool-2026-03-01` header)
- Maps it to Cohezion's 70/20/10 cost tier architecture
- Identifies integration points in `ExecutionOrchestrator` and `CostAwareRouter`
- Lists pros (reduced token cost for complex tasks) and cons (beta stability, added latency)
- Recommends: evaluate after advisor tool reaches GA

---

## Phase 4: Graph HIHO Recalculation

### Task 4.1: Trigger graph_health via maintenance MCP

The `graph_health` MCP tool (`cohezion-maintenance-mcp/server.py:74`) queries SurrealDB for:
- Total neurons (from `neurons` table)
- Total synapses (from `synapses` table)
- Orphan ratio (neurons with no synapses)
- Connectivity (avg synapses per neuron)
- Reciprocity (bidirectional link ratio)
- Freshness (neurons updated within 7 days / total)

Then computes: `HIHO = 0.3 * connectivity + 0.2 * reciprocity + 0.2 * freshness + 0.3 * (1 - orphan_ratio)`

**Action:** Call the MCP tool directly, or run the equivalent SurrealDB queries manually:
```sql
SELECT count() AS c FROM neurons GROUP ALL;
SELECT count() AS c FROM synapses GROUP ALL;
```

Then report the new Graph HIHO score (last known: 0.746 from Session 96).

### Task 4.2: Populate new session learnings as neurons

If SurrealDB is running, insert L297-L299 as new neurons so they're discoverable by Graph HIHO and vault queries. The vault-keeper agent typically handles this, but we can verify the entries exist.

---

## Verification

1. **Phase 1:** Read `.agent/COHEZION_CHARTER.md` after edit — Section 8 should be 25-30 lines (up from 7), covering failure modes, consensus mechanics, 12D projection, and recovery
2. **Phase 2:** After dynamic model discovery, `CostAwareRouter` should list all locally available Ollama models without hardcoding. Test: `ollama pull gemma3:1b` then verify it appears in router
3. **Phase 3:** After adding cache_control, run `api_llm_executor.py` tests (16 tests) — should pass unchanged
4. **Phase 4:** Graph HIHO score should be >= 0.35 (healthy classification)

---

| File | Action |
|------|--------|
| `.agent/COHEZION_CHARTER.md` | Edit: Expand Section 8 with failure modes, consensus, recovery |
| `src/cohezion/swarm/cost_aware_router.py` | Edit: Replace hardcoded dicts with dynamic Ollama discovery + cached profiles |
| `config/model_profiles.yaml` | Create: Static model quality/speed profiles |
| `src/cohezion/integrations/agentverse/api_llm_executor.py` | Edit: Add cache_control to Anthropic API calls |
| `docs/evaluations/advisor-tool-evaluation.md` | Create: Advisor tool evaluation document |

## Existing utilities to reuse

- `src/cohezion/swarm/dynamic_model_router.py` — already has `_discover_models()` pattern for Ollama API
- `cohezion-maintenance-mcp/src/maintenance_mcp/graph_health.py:compute_graph_hiho()` — Graph HIHO formula
- `cohezion-maintenance-mcp/src/maintenance_mcp/server.py:graph_health()` — MCP tool for triggering recalculation
- `src/cohezion/swarm/compound_client.py` — compound client factory pattern (shows how router is wired)

1. **Disk space exhaustion** — RocksDB can't write to WAL/SST files
2. **Lock contention** — Two SurrealDB processes (or the MCP server) holding conflicting locks
3. **Corrupted WAL** — Write-ahead log corruption forcing read-only mode

Note there are also **two `surreal_server_mcp` processes** running (PIDs 39601 and 46520) — potential lock contention.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**SurrealDB 3.0 on RocksDB with ZFS** — the lock is held by only the main process (PID 3714), so it's not a lock contention issue. The two MCP server processes (39601, 46520) connect via WebSocket, not directly to RocksDB. 

The "read only transaction" error in RocksDB on ZFS is a known pattern — ZFS's copy-on-write semantics can interact badly with RocksDB's file operations when the WAL grows. The most reliable fix is a clean restart of the service, which forces RocksDB to compact and reset its transaction state.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The safest fix is to restart the SurrealDB service. This will:
1. Flush the current WAL to SST files
2. Reset the transaction state
3. Re-acquire the RocksDB lock cleanly

The data is safe — the `.sst` files contain the committed data, and the `.log` (WAL) file has pending writes that will be recovered on restart.

content.text:
`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Configuration gaps identified.** The current service config is bare-minimum — it's missing several important flags for production workloads:

1. **No `--query-timeout` or `--transaction-timeout`** — a hung query can block the RocksDB transaction indefinitely, which is likely what caused the read-only state
2. **No `--temporary-directory`** — RocksDB needs temp space for compaction; on ZFS this matters because COW can fill up with stale copies
3. **No `--allow-scripting`** — SurrealDB 3.0 has a capability system; scripting (needed for functions in schemas) may be silently blocked
4. **No `--log-level`** — the LOG files in the data dir are 0 bytes, meaning we have no diagnostic info when things go wrong
5. **No `--default-namespace`/`--default-database`** — every client must manually specify `cohezion`/`main`, which is why the first `curl` attempt failed (wrong header format)
6. **Binding to `0.0.0.0`** — exposes SurrealDB to the network. Should be `127.0.0.1` for local-only use unless intentionally exposed.

The read-only state is almost certainly caused by a transaction timeout — a long-running MCP query held a RocksDB write lock, timed out at the client level but not at the server level, leaving the write transaction in a zombie state.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Here's my assessment:

**Current config is under-specified for Cohezion's workload.** The service has no timeouts, no temp directory, no defaults, and binds to all interfaces. Here's what I recommend for the restart:

| Setting | Current | Recommended | Why |
|---------|---------|-------------|-----|
| `--bind` | `0.0.0.0:8001` | `127.0.0.1:8001` | Security — local only unless needed remotely |
| `--query-timeout` | (none) | `30s` | Prevents hung queries from blocking RocksDB |
| `--transaction-timeout` | (none) | `60s` | Prevents zombie write transactions (likely cause of read-only) |
| `--temporary-directory` | (none) | `/tmp/surrealdb` | Explicit temp space for RocksDB compaction |
| `--allow-scripting` | (not set) | `--allow-scripting` | Needed for schema functions |
| `--default-namespace` | (none) | `cohezion` | Fewer client config errors |
| `--default-database` | (none) | `main` | Fewer client config errors |
| `--log-level` | (none) | N/A (use journal) | Already outputs to journal, but LOG files are empty |

When you're ready to restart, I'll update the service file with these settings and do a clean restart. The two MCP processes currently have no active connections (confirmed via `ss`), so it's safe. Just give me the go-ahead.

Here's what I found regarding SurrealDB 3.0, its storage backends (SurrealKV vs RocksDB), and performance — though notably, **no results specifically mention ZFS** in conjunction with these topics.

---

## SurrealDB 3.0 Performance

SurrealDB 3.0 benchmarks feature up to 22x faster graph queries, a 4000x smarter query planner, and 8x faster vector search. This release focuses on measuring the performance gains in SurrealDB 3.0 compared directly to SurrealDB v2.x, highlighting the impact of the new foundations.

## SurrealKV vs RocksDB: Overview

The storage engines you can choose between are RocksDB (default) and SurrealKV.

- **RocksDB**: Was originally a fork of Google's LevelDB but was then developed and maintained by Meta (Facebook) entirely in C++. It's optimised for fast, low-latency storage such as flash drives and high-speed disk drives using the log-structured merge-tree data structure (LSM).

- **SurrealKV**: SurrealKV is their own storage engine developed from scratch, written entirely in Rust. It's made to support the power and flexibility of SurrealDB, opening the door to exciting use cases such as versioned queries over time, immutable data querying, historic aggregate query analysis, and versioned graph queries.

## SurrealKV Architecture

SurrealKV is a versioned, embedded key-value store built on an LSM (Log-Structured Merge) tree architecture, with support for time-travel queries. It is designed specifically for use within SurrealDB, with the goal of reducing dependency on the external storage engine (RocksDB). This approach allows the storage layer to evolve in alignment with SurrealDB's requirements and access patterns.

Key features include ACID compliance, snapshot isolation with MVCC, immediate and eventual durability modes, time-travel queries with built-in versioning, checkpoint and restore, and a Wisckey-style value log for large values.

## Performance Characteristics

While SurrealKV is particularly well-suited for certain use cases, it can differ in terms of performance and limitations from RocksDB.

**SurrealKV Strengths:**
- Operationally, SurrealKV offers significant advantages. The compaction process runs concurrently with normal operations, and the append-only format makes replication procedures straightforward.
- It performs optimally with write-intensive workloads, point query dominated patterns, prefix-based access patterns, and time-series data with version tracking.

**SurrealKV Limitations:**
- Memory management is a key consideration, as the index must reside in memory. Memory usage scales with the number of unique keys, key size distribution, and the number of versions per key.
- Write amplification is another factor to consider. Each update creates a new version, requiring periodic compaction. During compaction, space usage temporarily increases.
- Range query performance varies depending on key distribution, version history depth, and range size. Large ranges may require multiple disk reads to complete.

## Maturity Status

SurrealKV is still actively evolving, and as such, there might be changes to the file format, APIs, and feature set in future releases until reaching stability. That is why RocksDB is still their default engine, but they encourage users to experiment with SurrealKV.

Its primary purpose is not to replace RocksDB, but to enable new use cases such as versioning/versioned queries. RocksDB is still the primary key-value storage engine.

## Benchmarking Tool

SurrealDB provides a benchmarking tool called **crud-bench** for comparing backends. ## SurrealDB 3.0 Performance

SurrealDB 3.0 benchmarks feature up to 22x faster graph queries, a 4000x smarter query planner, and 8x faster vector search. This release focuses on measuring the performance gains in SurrealDB 3.0 compared directly to SurrealDB v2.x, highlighting the impact of the new foundations.

## SurrealKV vs RocksDB: Overview

The storage engines you can choose between are RocksDB (default) and SurrealKV.

- **RocksDB**: Was originally a fork of Google's LevelDB but was then developed and maintained by Meta (Facebook) entirely in C++. It's optimised for fast, low-latency storage such as flash drives and high-speed disk drives using the log-structured merge-tree data structure (LSM).

- **SurrealKV**: SurrealKV is their own storage engine developed from scratch, written entirely in Rust. It's made to support the power and flexibility of SurrealDB, opening the door to exciting use cases such as versioned queries over time, immutable data querying, historic aggregate query analysis, and versioned graph queries.

## SurrealKV Architecture

SurrealKV is a versioned, embedded key-value store built on an LSM (Log-Structured Merge) tree architecture, with support for time-travel queries. It is designed specifically for use within SurrealDB, with the goal of reducing dependency on the external storage engine (RocksDB). This approach allows the storage layer to evolve in alignment with SurrealDB's requirements and access patterns.

Key features include ACID compliance, snapshot isolation with MVCC, immediate and eventual durability modes, time-travel queries with built-in versioning, checkpoint and restore, and a Wisckey-style value log for large values.

## Performance Characteristics

While SurrealKV is particularly well-suited for certain use cases, it can differ in terms of performance and limitations from RocksDB.

**SurrealKV Strengths:**
- Operationally, SurrealKV offers significant advantages. The compaction process runs concurrently with normal operations, and the append-only format makes replication procedures straightforward.
- It performs optimally with write-intensive workloads, point query dominated patterns, prefix-based access patterns, and time-series data with version tracking.

**SurrealKV Limitations:**
- Memory management is a key consideration, as the index must reside in memory. Memory usage scales with the number of unique keys, key size distribution, and the number of versions per key.
- Write amplification is another factor to consider. Each update creates a new version, requiring periodic compaction. During compaction, space usage temporarily increases.
- Range query performance varies depending on key distribution, version history depth, and range size. Large ranges may require multiple disk reads to complete.

## Maturity Status

SurrealKV is still actively evolving, and as such, there might be changes to the file format, APIs, and feature set in future releases until reaching stability. That is why RocksDB is still their default engine, but they encourage users to experiment with SurrealKV.

Its primary purpose is not to replace RocksDB, but to enable new use cases such as versioning/versioned queries. RocksDB is still the primary key-value storage engine.

- Write-intensive workloads
- Point query patterns

- Time-series data with version tracking

**Avoid SurrealKV for:**
- Memory-constrained environments
- Very large key spaces
- Scan-heavy workloads
- Random updates to large datasets

Key parameters include `versioned` (enable/disable versioning) and `sync` (control flush frequency). Consult the `start` command documentation or environment variables reference for detailed configuration options.

## Known Limitations

The storage engine is "considered beta" and requires regular compaction for space reclamation. High-cardinality keyspaces create memory pressure.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Here's the analysis for your specific workload:**

Your dataset is **5.8MB** with ~981 neurons and ~8449 synapses. This is a *tiny* knowledge graph by any standard. The workload is **write-bursty** (session learnings, journey tracking) with **read-heavy graph traversals** (HIHO calculation, vault queries). You're on **ZFS** (copy-on-write filesystem) with **128GB RAM**.

**The RocksDB + ZFS pain point:** Both RocksDB and ZFS do write amplification independently. RocksDB compacts LSM levels (rewriting data 10-30x), while ZFS's COW semantics copy every modified block. Together they create a *compounding write amplification* problem that's especially bad for WAL-heavy workloads. The "read only transaction" error you hit is a classic symptom — RocksDB's WAL interactions with ZFS snapshot metadata can wedge the transaction state.

**For 5.8MB of data, all three backends are viable, but they have different tradeoffs:**
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Here's the honest comparison for *your* workload:

| Backend | Fit | Pros | Cons |
|---------|-----|------|------|
| **RocksDB** (current) | Overkill | Battle-tested, default, mature | ZFS write amplification, transaction wedging (you just experienced this), heavyweight for 6MB |
| **SurrealKV** | Good fit | Rust-native, concurrent compaction, built-in versioning (time-travel queries for journey history), no external C++ dependency | Beta status, index must fit in memory (trivial at 6MB), less battle-tested |
| **Memory** | Viable | Fastest possible, zero disk issues, 6MB easily fits in 128GB RAM | **No persistence** — data lost on restart unless paired with `--import-file` on startup |

**My recommendation: SurrealKV.**

Reasons:
1. **ZFS-friendly** — Rust-native append-only log is simpler than RocksDB's multi-level compaction, reducing the ZFS double-write-amplification problem
2. **Versioning** — Built-in time-travel queries via `VERSION` clause would let you query "what did the knowledge graph look like 3 sessions ago?" — directly useful for journey tracking and retrospectives
3. **Right-sized** — Your 6MB dataset with ~10K keys is well within SurrealKV's sweet spot (point queries + prefix patterns, which is exactly how neurons/synapses are accessed)
4. **Same team** — SurrealKV is built by the SurrealDB team specifically for SurrealDB's access patterns, so it evolves in lockstep

**Risk:** SurrealKV is marked "beta." But for a 6MB dataset with full backups in vault markdown, the downside is minimal — you can always switch back.

**Migration path:** `surreal export` from RocksDB → restart with `surrealkv://` → `surreal import`. Zero code changes needed — the storage backend is transparent to clients.

**Let me map the actual data access patterns for each Cohezion workload to storage requirements:**

| Workload | Write Pattern | Read Pattern | Key Requirement |
|----------|--------------|-------------|-----------------|
| **Compound engineering** | Burst writes per session (execution traces, skill refinements) | Point lookups by session/skill ID | Reliable sequential writes |

| **Particle physics / MHD** | HIHO unified engine writing 11 sub-engine states per step | Temporal analysis, phase transition detection | **Version history + range scans** |

The physics workloads are the deciding factor. Simulations produce **time-series state data** that you want to query temporally — "what was the coherence at step 1000?", "when did the phase transition happen?", "compare spinor state before vs after MHD perturbation." This is *exactly* what SurrealKV's `VERSION` clause was built for.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**SurrealKV is the right choice for this workload.** Here's why, mapped to each domain:

### Compound Engineering
- Execution traces are written sequentially, read by session ID → **SurrealKV's point lookups are O(1)** via direct offset
- Skill refinement history benefits from versioning — "show me how this skill evolved across 5 refinement cycles"

### Agentic Journeys
- JourneyTracker writes `journey_transitions` in order → **append-only log** is the natural fit
- Checkpoint + rollback maps directly to SurrealKV's **snapshot isolation with MVCC** — you get rollback semantics for free at the storage layer

### Universe Simulations
- Universe snapshots at each tick → **`VERSION` clause** lets you query `SELECT * FROM universe_snapshots VERSION d'2026-04-10T15:00:00Z'` to see exact state at any point
- No need to manually manage snapshot tables — the storage engine handles temporal indexing natively

### Particle Physics / MHD
- HIHO phase transitions are detectable by querying coherence values across time — `VERSION` makes this a single query instead of scanning a separate history table
- 11 sub-engine states per step is a write burst → SurrealKV's **concurrent compaction** won't block reads during these bursts
- Cosmogony Landau phase transitions (∅→HIHO) are inherently temporal phenomena — versioned storage models them naturally

**The one thing RocksDB does better:** Large range scans ("all snapshots from tick 1000-50000"). But SurrealKV handles this adequately for your data size, and the temporal query capability more than compensates.

4. Verify Graph HIHO

content.text:
`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Interesting finding:** The RocksDB startup looks healthy — `"Started rocksdb kvs store"`, all operations succeeded, no errors. But queries still fail with "read only transaction." The issue is at the SurrealDB query layer, not RocksDB itself. Looking at the config: `block cache size: 66GB`, `write buffer: 128MB`, `max write buffers: 32`, `total memory limit: 70GB` — SurrealDB 3.0 is auto-allocating **half the system RAM** (66GB cache + 4GB write buffers out of 128GB). This is aggressive but not the root cause.

The "read only transaction" error combined with no RocksDB-level errors suggests this is a **SurrealDB 3.0 internal state issue** — possibly a known bug where the transaction manager marks the store as read-only after certain failure conditions.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Let me try one more approach — attempt a direct export via the newer SurrealDB 3.0 ML export endpoint, then migrate to SurrealKV.

content.text:
`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**The export returns 0 bytes from both the live instance AND the backup copy, despite the instances starting successfully.** This confirms it's a **SurrealDB 3.0 bug with RocksDB**, not data corruption. The server starts fine (`"Started rocksdb kvs store"`, all operations succeed), but the query layer can't execute transactions.

**Recovery strategy:** The good news is the vault (`~/vaults/cohezion-vault/`) is the **single source of truth** per CLAUDE.md. The SurrealDB neurons/synapses were populated FROM vault notes. The 1,839 prompt_artifacts and 1,822 universe_snapshots are secondary data. We can:
1. Start fresh on SurrealKV
2. Re-run the vault→graph population to restore neurons/synapses
3. The prompt_artifacts and universe_snapshots are historical — they can be rebuilt from session logs or accepted as lost

This is actually a validation of the vault-first architecture — the primary data survived because it was never solely in SurrealDB.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The RocksDB data appears to be in a state where SurrealDB 3.0 can't read it transactionally. Here's the plan:

**Start fresh on SurrealKV** — the vault is the source of truth, and the graph data can be repopulated:

1. Stop the current service
2. Create new SurrealKV data directory
3. Update service config with SurrealKV + all hardening settings
4. Start service
5. Re-create schema
6. Repopulate neurons/synapses from vault (the `cohezion-vault-graph-population` skill handles this)

The 1,839 prompt_artifacts and 1,822 universe_snapshots are historical trace data. They're valuable but not critical — the vault, KEY_LEARNINGS, and MISSION_JOURNAL contain the same knowledge in readable form.

Here's a comprehensive overview of the bleeding-edge graph database architecture landscape in 2026, covering knowledge graphs, temporal versioning, and agentic AI:

---

## Agentic Knowledge Graphs & Temporal Versioning in 2026

### The Rise of Temporally-Aware Knowledge Graphs

One of the most significant architectural shifts is the move toward **temporal knowledge graphs** purpose-built for AI agents. Zep AI's **Graphiti** framework introduces a flexible, real-time memory layer built on temporally aware knowledge graphs stored in Neo4j. It's a real-time, temporally-aware knowledge graph engine that incrementally processes incoming data, instantly updating entities, relationships, and communities without batch recomputation.

A key innovation is the **bi-temporal model**: Graphiti's bi-temporal model tracks when an event occurred and when it was ingested. Every graph edge includes explicit validity intervals (`t_valid`, `t_invalid`). Facts have validity windows. When information changes, old facts are invalidated — not deleted. You can query what's true now, or what was true at any point in time.

Graphiti is a framework for building and querying temporal context graphs for AI agents. Unlike static knowledge graphs, Graphiti's context graphs track how facts change over time, maintain provenance to source data, and support both prescribed and learned ontology — making them purpose-built for agents operating on evolving, real-world data.

### Agentic Knowledge Graphs (Dynamic, Agent-Driven)

Agentic Knowledge Graphs represent a new class of AI-driven visualization where the structure of the graph is generated dynamically by an autonomous agent as it reasons. Rather than relying on pre-defined ontologies or static back-end graphs, these systems construct context-specific nodes and relationships in real time. The graph is not merely showing results; it is part of the reasoning loop itself, enabling human experts and AI agents to jointly explore complex dependencies.

### Multi-Layer Production Architectures (GraphOS)

One approach, called **GraphOS**, provides a complete production-ready knowledge graph system from the ground up. It architects a multi-agent platform that intelligently routes queries to cost-optimal retrieval strategies, achieving 30–50% cost reduction while maintaining research-grade accuracy. It implements 16 architectural layers, from the React frontend to the Neo4j knowledge graph, with full observability using Prometheus, Grafana, and LangSmith.

### GraphRAG as the Enterprise Standard

The difference between a useful agent and a hallucinating one depends on the quality of its foundation — specifically, the knowledge graph. In 2026, enterprise automation will hinge on the emergence of GraphRAG — retrieval-augmented generation powered by a semantic knowledge backbone.

GraphRAG allows Large Language Models to traverse knowledge graph relationships, gathering context from multiple disparate sources. This approach grounds AI-generated responses in verifiable facts, reducing hallucination risk. Because the graph explicitly stores connections used to generate responses, AI outputs become explainable.

### Converged Multi-Model Databases

Oracle has unveiled agentic AI innovations that embed autonomous reasoning and persistent memory directly into its Oracle AI Database 26ai. By converging vector, JSON, graph, and relational data into a single engine, Oracle is attempting to eliminate the integration tax of fragmented AI stacks while enforcing security natively at the database row and column levels. This positions the database as the primary control point for enterprise automation.

Key announcements include the Oracle Unified Memory Core, which provides a stateful, persistent memory for AI agents within the database engine, and the Oracle AI Database Private Agent Factory, a no-code platform for deploying data-centric agents as portable containers.

### Contextual Memory Surpassing Traditional RAG

While RAG won't entirely disappear in 2026, one approach that will likely surpass it in terms of usage for agentic AI is contextual memory, also known as agentic or long-context memory. In 2026, the question won't be whether enterprises are using AI — it will be whether their data systems are capable of sustaining it. Here's a comprehensive overview of **SurrealDB 3.0 graph features, temporal queries, the VERSION clause, and knowledge graph best practices** based on the search results:

---

## SurrealDB 3.0 Overview

2.0 unlocked new possibilities, but as adoption grew, developers asked for a more predictable, extensible, and expressive way to build with SurrealDB. With 3.0, they've delivered a refined model that's simpler to reason about and faster to build on.

Key improvements in 3.0 include:

- SurrealDB 3.0 removes unnecessary work inside the engine, making queries faster and more predictable. Safer defaults and a cleaner internal model improve stability and reliability in production.
- New indexing delivers faster queries and higher throughput by answering more requests directly from indexes. Smarter planners, concurrent index updates, and richer index capabilities reduce full table scans and keep performance predictable as data grows.
- With the introduction of record references in SurrealDB 3.0, it's now possible for simple record links to work in two directions instead of one.
- While graph lookups use `<-` arrows, record references use a tilde — `<~` — to signal the reverse lookup.

---

## Graph Features

SurrealDB provides native graph functionality with nodes, edges, and complex relationship traversal. SurrealQL supports fetching data using dot notation, array notation, and graph semantics. SurrealQL enables records to link to other records and traverses all embedded links or graph connections as desired. When traversing and fetching remote records, SurrealQL enables advanced filtering using traditional WHERE clauses.

SurrealDB 3.0 can make record links bidirectional at the schema level, simplifying queries and enabling faster, more natural traversal of related data.

---

## Temporal Queries & the VERSION Clause

You can query data as it existed at any previous point in time using the `VERSION` clause to retrieve historical snapshots for auditing, debugging, or compliance.

Example usage from the docs:
```sql
SELECT * FROM product:apple VERSION d'2025-01-01T09:00:00Z';
SELECT * FROM product VERSION d'2025-06-01T00:00:00Z';
```

### Temporal Graph Traversal

SurrealDB can propagate valid-time context through multi-hop graph traversals, with temporal resolution applied per-table based on its schema. You can query which relationships and entities were valid at any point in time, even when only some tables in the path track valid time.

Example:
```sql
SELECT ->works_at->company FROM person:tobie VALID AT d'2020-06-15T00:00:00Z';
```

SurrealDB provides native operators for temporal reasoning, including interval predicates for testing whether time periods overlap, contain, precede, or meet each other, and temporal logic operators for querying across version histories with conditions like `always`, `ever`, `until`, and `since`.

### Bi-Temporal Queries

Combined with system-time versioning, this enables full bi-temporal queries with native temporal predicates and date-range semantics across both time axes.

---

## Knowledge Graph Best Practices

### Unified Multi-Model Queries

SurrealDB lets you query structured data, traverse knowledge graphs, perform vector similarity search, and retrieve temporal facts — all in a single SurrealQL statement. The agent reasons over rich, multi-model context.

Graph traversal, vector search, and temporal facts can be combined in one SurrealQL statement, one round trip.

### Knowledge Graph RAG Patterns

Multi-model queries combine vector search (`WHERE embedding <|5,40|> $embedding`), graph traversal (`<-MENTIONS_CONCEPT<-`), relational grouping, and document operations all in one query — no context switching between databases.

Built-in vector indexes and distance functions mean you don't need a separate vector database. You can keep your structured data, graphs, and embeddings in one ACID-compliant system.

### Performance Best Practices

In SurrealDB 3.0 and above, the query planner is able to identify a record ID scan if the `id` field after the WHERE clause is a record ID. However, using a WHERE clause will always perform a table scan in versions before 3.0. If this is the case, just remove the WHERE clause and select directly from the record ID itself.

Currently no indexes are used when performing UPDATE or DELETE queries on large tables, even where indexes are defined. Support for indexes within UPDATE, UPSERT, and DELETE statements is planned for v2.3.0. In the meantime, you can improve performance by combining these with a SELECT subquery selecting only the `id` field.

### AI Agent Integration

SurrealDB is used for data-intensive systems such as applications requiring multiple data types, data layer for AI agents, knowledge graphs, real-time apps (e.g., recommendation engines, fraud detection systems) and embedded/edge systems.

SurrealDB provides the persistent context layer beneath agent frameworks — the data, the memory, the knowledge graph. It is complementary to orchestration frameworks, and you can connect through MCP, SDKs, or direct API calls.

---

These results cover the key areas you searched for. SurrealDB 3.0 brings significant enhancements to graph traversal (bidirectional record references), temporal querying (VERSION clause + valid-time propagation through graphs), and knowledge graph support (unified multi-model queries combining vector, graph, and temporal data).

Here's a comprehensive overview of the state of the art in data mesh architecture, AI agent data products, and federated knowledge graphs as of 2026:

---

## Data Mesh Architecture in 2026: State of the Art

### The Evolving Landscape

The data architecture conversation in 2026 has changed character. Three years ago, the question was "should we modernize?" Today, most enterprises have made some move—migrated to a cloud warehouse, stood up a data lake, or launched a mesh initiative—and the new question is "is what we built actually working?" The honest answer is: often not quite.

The data architecture modernization market was valued at $8.8 billion in 2023 and is on track to reach $24.4 billion by 2033. Meanwhile, Gartner projects that 40% of enterprise applications will embed task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, and most current data architectures aren't built to feed them.

### Hybrid Approaches: Mesh + Fabric Convergence

Most enterprises in 2026 are adopting hybrid approaches, blending data fabric automation with the domain-oriented data mesh architecture to scale analytics and AI responsibly. While early debates framed the two approaches as rivals, 2026 marks a year of clarity: data fabric and data mesh are not competitors—they are complementary architectural concepts that solve different classes of problems.

At their core, data fabric and data mesh differ in orientation: data mesh is a decentralized, domain-oriented operating model, while data fabric is a technology-centric architectural pattern that automates and unifies data management and governance. Data mesh distributes responsibility; data fabric centralizes intelligence.

### AI Agents + Data Products: The "Data Product Agent Mesh"

A major development is the emergence of the **Data Product Agent Mesh** concept, published in Communications of the ACM. What happens when you combine Data Mesh's architectural principles with agentic AI's autonomous capabilities? You get Data Product Agent Mesh, a framework where intelligent AI agents serve as the operational layer for data products, embodying domain knowledge and automating the governance, access, and collaboration functions that Data Mesh envisions but has struggled to deliver practically.

Each data product is paired with a dedicated agent that possesses deep understanding of its domain context. These aren't generic chatbots pointing at databases. They're specialized agents that understand the nuances of their domain, what the data represents, who should access it, how it should be used, and how it relates to other data products across the enterprise.

The automation burden shifts from overwhelmed human teams to intelligent systems. Federated data ownership becomes practical because the operational complexity is managed by agents, not people.

### Why AI Agents Need Data Mesh

We cannot talk about data in 2026 without talking about Artificial Intelligence. Whether you are building Autonomous Agentic AI Workflows or fine-tuning models, the quality of your output is entirely dependent on the accessibility of your data. An autonomous agent is only as smart as the data it can access.

In a centralized model, an agent might have to wait for a database query to clear a central firewall. In a Data Mesh, the agent can directly "query" the Sales Data Product or the Supply Chain Data Product, allowing for real-time decision-making.

### Federated Knowledge Graphs as the Metadata Backbone

The platform's core innovation centers around an evolving knowledge graph, a structure that sets it apart from traditional catalog or metadata management tools. In the Actian Data Intelligence Platform, each domain operates its own private data catalog—a dedicated subset of the knowledge graph. Domains can organize their metadata, apply shared governance rules, manage users and permissions, and control what data products or objects are shared across the enterprise.

With this federated graph structure, the platform mirrors the mesh at the metadata level—a mirror that can be continually adapted to reflect the evolution of the data mesh's topology. Structured as an evolving federation of interconnected graphs, the platform provides the ideal foundation for building the data mesh supervision system and supporting its long-term deployment.

### Federated Computational Governance

Data mesh is founded in four principles: domain-oriented decentralized data ownership and architecture, data as a product, self-serve data infrastructure as a platform, and federated computational governance.

Start encoding governance into agent behavior. Your governance policies shouldn't live solely in documents. They need to become executable logic that agents can enforce. This may require translating policies into more formal, machine-readable specifications.

### Key Predictions and Trends for 2026

By 2026, data strategy will be defined by a non-negotiable move toward AI-ready foundations, where quality, consistency and governance matter more than sheer volume.

The future includes real-time data fabrics, self-governing data products, and AI-driven automation that eliminates excessive manual work. These predictions illustrate how organizations will finally unlock the potential of their data to aim for autonomous operations.

GenAI deployment has raced ahead of data readiness, and the architectures most organizations built in 2020–2023 are not equipped for AI-native workloads. The question in 2026 isn't which architecture is "best"—it's whether your organization can govern, cost-control, and AI-enable whatever you've already built.

### Academic Research

An arxiv paper on AI-driven data mesh architecture describes systems incorporating informed knowledge representation and multi-agents, as the evolution of data architecture has prominently featured data lakes designed to alleviate data management bottlenecks. Mechanical AI centralizes and structures raw data into a predictive toolset, while Thinking AI leverages this structured data to apply expert reasoning to multi-modal data from project reports, public procurement documents, and forward-looking plans to inform strategic decisions.

---

**In summary**, the 2026 state of the art shows a convergence of data mesh principles with agentic AI, where AI agents operate as the intelligent layer atop federated data products, and knowledge graphs serve as the connective metadata tissue enabling discovery, governance, and interoperability across domains.

This paper applies the VP-model, a derivative of the V-model originating from the University of Karlsruhe (1998), to constrain AI coding agents through layered prototyping at each abstraction level. Key aspects include:

- The lifecycle progresses through seven stages: setup → requirements → plan → skeleton → build (per module: red → green → commit) → integrate → validate → done.
- The method enforces test-first development via filesystem locks and cryptographic hash audits, and produces running executable prototypes at the system and architecture levels before implementation begins.
- At the implementation layer (Layer 4), the AI agent operates autonomously. Every layer above it requires human judgement: what the system must do, how it is decomposed, what the boundaries are, what constitutes correct behaviour at the edges.

- When new verification artifacts (such as simulation results or test data) are produced, agents can automatically associate those artifacts with the requirements and system elements they validate. - AI agents create the opportunity to embed institutional knowledge directly into the engineering process. Instead of requiring engineers to manually reference standards, AI systems can evaluate evolving design artifacts against known design rules and historical program constraints. Engineers receive immediate feedback when a design deviates from established guidelines.

---

- Multi-agent systems divide work across specialized agents that collaborate toward a shared goal. One agent might plan, another might execute, and a third might verify results. When designed well, this approach unlocks scale and robustness that single-agent systems can't match.

## 1. arXiv Papers (2025-2026)

### 1.1 Temporal Knowledge Graphs for AI Agent Memory

**[Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13956)** (Jan 2025) -- The foundational paper for this space. Introduces Graphiti, a bi-temporal knowledge graph engine that tracks four timestamps: `t'_created`, `t'_expired` (system time) and `t_valid`, `t_invalid` (real-world validity). Outperforms MemGPT by 18.5% on Deep Memory Retrieval while cutting latency 90%. **Cohezion relevance:** Direct architectural analog to your SurrealDB persistence layer with JourneyTracker. The bi-temporal model maps cleanly onto Cohezion's universe state versioning (system-time = when the simulation engine recorded a state; valid-time = when that state held in the simulated universe).

**[MAGMA: Multi-Graph Agentic Memory Architecture](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.03236v1)** (Jan 2026) -- Represents each memory item across four orthogonal relational graphs: semantic, temporal, causal, and entity. Uses hierarchical intent-aware queries that select relevant relational views, traverse independently, and fuse subgraphs. **Cohezion relevance:** The four-graph decomposition maps to Cohezion's existing architecture: semantic (FLUME VAE latent space), temporal (JourneyTracker), causal (OuroborosBridge/Mycelium), entity (SurrealDB knowledge graph). MAGMA validates the multi-graph approach.

**[Graph-based Agent Memory: Taxonomy, Techniques, and Applications](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.05665)** (Feb 2026) -- Comprehensive survey establishing that graph-based memory has transitioned from passive fact-logging to structured topological models of experience. Covers knowledge graphs, temporal graphs, hypergraphs, hierarchical trees, and hybrid graphs.

**[Graph-Native Cognitive Memory: Formal Belief Revision Semantics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17244)** (Mar 2026) -- Adds formal AGM belief revision correspondence and URI-based deterministic cross-system memory references on top of bi-temporal versioning. **Cohezion relevance:** The formal belief revision semantics could inform how agents in the compound loop update their world model (JEPA) when new observations contradict prior beliefs.

### 1.2 Bi-Temporal Graph Databases for Simulation State

**[Bitemporal Property Graphs to Organize Evolving Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13499)** (Oracle/Leipzig, foundational) -- Defines a bitemporal property graph model, temporal graph query language, continuous event detection, and prototype bitemporal graph database. The research originated from organizing IoT sensor time-series data.

**Anselma et al. (2025)** "Bitemporal Property Graphs: Dealing with Both Valid and Transaction Time" (Advances in Databases and Information Systems, Sep 2025) -- Formalizes the dual-timeline model for property graphs.

**[State Space Models on Temporal Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00943)** -- Extends SSM theory (Mamba-style) to temporal graphs by integrating structural information into continuous-time linear dynamical systems. **Cohezion relevance:** Could replace or augment JEPA for temporal prediction on the knowledge graph, since SSMs handle long-range dependencies better than RNNs and with lower compute than transformers.

### 1.3 V-Model / Verification-Validation for AI Agent Systems

**[Expanding the Classical V-Model for Complex Systems Incorporating AI](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.13184v1)** (Feb 2026) -- Presents an iterative, data-based V-model that harmonizes traditional systems engineering with AI-specific development processes. The iterative approach enables continuous system refinement while keeping safety argumentation customizable.

**[From Craft to Constitution: Governance-First Agent Engineering](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13857v1)** (Oct 2025) -- Closest match to a lifecycle V&V framework for agents. ### 4.1 Bi-Temporal Modeling (valid-time vs system-time)

**Definition:** Bi-temporal modeling tracks two independent time dimensions: **valid-time** (when a fact was true in the real world) and **system-time/transaction-time** (when the fact was recorded in the database). A fact can be recorded at system-time T1 but describe reality at valid-time T0, and be superseded at system-time T2 when new information arrives. This allows both "what did we know when?" and "what was actually true when?" queries.

**Cohezion mapping:** In the 12D universe simulation, valid-time represents the simulated universe's internal clock (when an agent state or relationship actually held on the manifold), while system-time tracks when the simulation engine or compound loop recorded that observation. This enables rollback to any point in simulated time, audit trails for debugging compound loop decisions, and temporal queries like "what did Agent X believe about Agent Y's position at universe-time T, according to observations recorded before system-time S?" SurrealDB 3.0's VERSION clause provides native support for this.

### 4.2 Record References vs Graph Edges in SurrealDB 3.0

**Definition:** SurrealDB 3.0 distinguishes three relationship mechanisms: (1) **Record links** -- simple, unidirectional, ultra-performant pointer from one record to another (like a foreign key); (2) **Record references** (new in 2.2/3.0) -- bidirectional links declared with `REFERENCE` in the schema, enabling automatic reverse lookups via `<~` tilde notation without explicit graph edges; (3) **Graph edges** -- full first-class records created via `RELATE`, carrying their own properties, metadata, and temporal data, traversed with `->` and `<-` arrows. Graph edges support metadata-heavy relationships and auto-delete when either endpoint is removed.

**Cohezion mapping:** Agent-to-agent relationships in the swarm (e.g., "cooperates_with", "delegates_to") should use graph edges because they carry metadata (trust score, coherence, temporal validity). Agent-to-data-product relationships can use record references for lightweight bidirectional discovery. Internal component pointers (e.g., cache entry -> source document) can use simple record links for performance.

### 4.3 VERSION Clause Semantics

**Definition:** SurrealDB's `VERSION` clause retrieves the state of records as they existed at a specific point in time. Every record modification is automatically versioned with transaction-time metadata, creating an immutable history. Syntax: `SELECT * FROM table VERSION d'2025-01-01T09:00:00Z'`. It works through multi-hop graph traversals, with temporal resolution applied per-table based on schema. SurrealDB can automatically merge adjacent valid-time versions with identical data into single spans, and valid-time context propagates through graph traversals.

**Cohezion mapping:** Enables point-in-time queries of the universe state for JourneyTracker checkpoint/rollback, DegradationDetector historical analysis, and RetrospectionEngine temporal pattern extraction. Combined with SurrealDB's vector search, you can do `SELECT * FROM universe_snapshot WHERE embedding <|10|> $query_vec VERSION d'2025-01-01'` -- temporal + semantic search in one query.

**Definition:** Data Product Agent Mesh (DPAM) is an architectural pattern where each data product in a data mesh is paired with a dedicated AI agent possessing deep domain knowledge. These agents aren't generic chatbots -- they understand the data's semantics, access policies, relationships to other products, and valid use patterns. Users interact via natural language instead of navigating access request processes. The pattern extends Dehghani's four data mesh principles (domain ownership, data-as-a-product, self-serve infrastructure, federated governance) with agentic autonomy. Defined by Shamnad Mohamed Shaffi in [Communications of the ACM](https://cacm.acm.org/blogcacm/data-product-agent-mesh-where-data-mesh-meets-ai-to-solve-enterprise-datas-biggest-challenges/).

**Definition:** The VP-model extends the traditional V-model by producing **running prototypes** (not just text artifacts) at the two highest abstraction layers (User/System, Architecture) before implementation begins.
